analysis.one_liner: Lets employers refuse to hire union organizers who apply for jobs to organize workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let employers refuse to hire paid union organizers, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: For decades, unions have used a tactic called "salting": a trained, paid union organizer applies for a job at a nonunion company, gets hired, and then organizes the workforce from the inside. Federal labor law has treated this as legal, and employers cannot legally refuse to hire someone because they are a paid organizer. This bill would change the National Labor Relations Act so that an employer could refuse to hire anyone whose real purpose in applying was organizing. It would make it much harder for unions to organize nonunion workplaces, which is exactly where most new organizing happens.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially nonunion companies that have avoided unionization. The bill would give them a legal basis to screen out paid union organizers before they ever get in the door, removing one of the main tools unions use to organize nonunion workplaces. Unionized competitors would also benefit, since organizing drives at nonunion rivals are a common way unions try to level the playing field.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a sentence to the National Labor Relations Act stating that nothing in the ban on employer unfair labor practices requires an employer to hire someone who sought the job 'in furtherance of other employment or agency status' — in plain terms, a paid union organizer working for a union or agency. [S2] [S3]

The bill's stated purpose is to relieve pressure on employers to hire people who, in Congress's findings, seek jobs to 'disrupt the workplace' or 'inflict economic harm' designed to put the employer out of business — the bill's characterization of the practice known as salting. [S3]

If enacted, an employer could decline to hire a known or suspected organizer without facing the unfair-labor-practice charge that current law allows, effectively ending the ability of unions to place organizers inside target companies. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Workers and unions. The people who bear the cost are employees at nonunion workplaces who want to join a union, because the bill removes one of the few proven ways to organize them: an organizer who becomes a coworker first. It also gives anti-union employers a ready-made reason to reject any applicant they suspect of union sympathies, since motive can be hard to prove either way.

drawbacks.text: The bill's core effect is to make it legal to refuse employment based on the applicant's union-related purpose. Because a motive is easy to allege and hard to disprove, employers could use the exemption to reject applicants suspected of union sympathy generally, beyond the paid-organizer cases the bill describes. [S3]

The bill states it 'preserve[s] the rights of workers to organize' while removing the tactic through which unions most often organize nonunion workplaces, where the large majority of American workers are employed; critics of similar proposals have argued these two purposes cannot both hold. [S3]

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill changes settled law: the National Labor Relations Board has long treated refusing to hire a paid organizer because they are an organizer as discrimination based on union activity, which the Act prohibits; this bill would carve that practice out. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit, on its own terms, is real but narrow: employers gain protection from a tactic they consider coercive, and some organizers do seek jobs to generate strikes or organizing drives rather than to do the work. The cost falls on workers' ability to form unions at all in nonunion companies, since the bill targets the standard method of reaching them. On balance, the bill's gains flow to employers and its losses to workers' organizing rights, which is why it drew no cosponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King of Iowa introduced the bill on April 25, 2013, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. [S5] [S1]
On July 8, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions — the last action ever taken on it. [S5]
The bill had zero cosponsors, including none from its own party. [S4]
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015, so the bill died without a hearing, a markup, or any vote. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nonunion employers are better off, because the organizing tool the bill would have restricted remains available — though the bill's death was near-certain from the start given its single sponsor and zero cosponsors. Workers' existing legal right to organize through salting was untouched.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleague in either party joined him.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: John Kline, R-MN)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to a subcommittee on July 8, 2013, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died there. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no recorded opposition; the only visible fact is that a single House Republican sponsored the bill and not one other member of either party cosponsored it. [S4]

industries.note: The bill would give employers a new legal defense for refusing to hire union organizers, protecting them from unfair-labor-practice liability. The gain comes directly at the expense of workers' ability to organize those same workplaces.

Salting is a core method unions use to organize nonunion companies, where most American workers are employed; the bill would shut that door. Unions' interest in defeating the bill runs with workers' interest in being able to join one.
